content.paragraph: In defining a definite integral $${\int_{a}^{b}{f(x)}}dx$$ we dealt with a function $$f$$ defined on a finite interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ and we assumed that $$f$$ does not have an infinite discontinuity (see Section 5.2). In this section we extend the concept of a definite integral to the case where the interval is infinite and also to the case where $$f$$ has an infinite discontinuity in $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ . In either case the integral is called an improper integral. One of the most important applications of this idea, probability distributions, will be studied in Section 8.5.

subsection.title: A Comparison Test for Improper Integrals
subsection.paragraph: Sometimes it is impossible to find the exact value of an improper integral and yet it is important to know whether the integral is convergent or divergent. In such cases the following theorem is useful. Although we state it for Type 1 integrals, a similar theorem is true for Type 2 integrals.

note.title: Comparison Theorem
note.paragraph: Suppose that $$f$$ and $$g$$ are continuous functions with $$f(x) \geqslant g(x) \geqslant 0$$ for $$x \geqslant a$$ .

item.paragraph: If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is convergent, then $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is convergent.
If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is divergent, then $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is divergent.

subsection.paragraph: We omit the proof of the Comparison Theorem, but Figure 12 makes it seem plausible. If the area under the top curve $$y = f(x)$$ is finite, then so is the area under the bottom curve $$y = g(x)$$ . And if the area under $$y = g(x)$$ is infinite, then so is the area under $$y = f(x)$$ . [Note that the reverse is not necessarily true: If $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ is convergent, $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ may or may not be convergent, and if $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{f(x)}}dx$$ is divergent, $${\int_{a}^{\infty}{g(x)}}dx$$ may or may not be divergent.]

In Exercise 84 we indicate how to show that its value is approximately $$0.8862$$ . In probability theory it is important to know the exact value of this improper integral, as we will see in Section 8.5; using the methods of multivariable calculus it can be shown that the exact value is $$\sqrt{\pi} \slash 2$$ . Table 1 illustrates the definition of a convergent improper integral by showing how the (computer-generated) values of $${\int_{0}^{t}e^{- x^{2}}}dx$$ approach $$\sqrt{\pi} \slash 2$$ as $$t$$ becomes large. In fact, these values converge quite quickly because $$\left. e^{- x^{2}}\rightarrow 0 \right.$$ very rapidly as $$\left. x\rightarrow\infty \right.$$ .
